gap: No result ChatGPT got states how these skimmers keep charged without a plug: when the battery runs low, the robot drives itself into a sunny patch of the pool and charges there. Betta's own support also says that in fall and winter 'even bright days may not provide enough solar energy because of the lower sun angle', and that a full solar charge takes 6 hours to a full day of direct sun.
standout_why: I checked the three cited pages. The Hook Up test (thesmarthomehookup.com/test_install/solar-pool-skimmers-…) has measured drain and gain rates and the sun hours each model needs to run nonstop (Aiper about 5.7 h, iSkim about 6.6 h). It does not say how a skimmer gets itself into the sun, and it says nothing about season or sun angle. The Hook Up recommendation page lists picks and prices and mentions only the iSkim's $25 wall charger. It also says nothing on sun-seeking or season. Robotdoorstep (cited) says shade from a lanai roof or screen 'cuts panel output, so a plug-in charge option matters'. It does not cover sun-seeking, sun angle or Betta's SE vs SE Plus charging. ChatGPT's answer had only a generic line about cloudy days and shade. Today is 2026-11-17, so the low winter sun angle applies right now.
decides: The finding confirms that a solar-only skimmer like the Betta SE can work without a plug, but only if part of the pool gets several hours of direct sun every day, because the robot has to park there to charge. In November through winter, Betta itself warns that solar alone may fall short. A shopper who wants it to keep working without ever plugging in should pick a model with a plug-in backup for winter, and should know what each one needs. The Aiper EcoSurfer S2 comes with a DC charger. Betta's FAQ names the SE Plus as the model with dual charging. The Beatbot iSkim's adapter costs $25 extra, per The Hook Up. The plain Betta SE suits a pool with full sun in summer.

findings.label: How it charges when low, without a plug
findings.value: Parks itself in a sunny area and charges when the battery falls below a set level; no need to take it out of the pool
findings.source_title: Betta support: Betta seems to be out of charge, do I need to take it out of the pool and leave it in some bright spot?
findings.note: I could not open this page myself (WebFetch returned 404). The text comes from the search engine's summary of it: 'As long as there is an area in the pool that has good direct sunlight during the day, Betta will stop in the area and charge up when the remaining charge of the battery is below its set level.' The same behaviour is implied by the two Betta FAQ articles I did open. Re-open this page before publishing.

findings.label: Solar charging in fall/winter
findings.value: Fall/winter sun may not be enough even on bright days, because of the lower sun angle
findings.source_title: Why doesn't my Betta hold a charge, won't charge, or shows signs of a degraded or dead battery?
findings.note: Betta's wording: 'during fall and winter, even bright days may not provide enough solar energy because of the lower sun angle.' A blinking red light 'usually means your Betta isn't receiving enough sunlight'. Article modified 2025-12-09.

findings.label: Full solar charge from depleted
findings.value: 6 hours to a full day of direct sun, unit tilted about 45°, gives about 30 h of runtime
findings.source_title: Why doesn't my Betta hold a charge, won't charge, or shows signs of a degraded or dead battery?
findings.note: Betta's instructions: place it outdoors 'at a slight angle (around 45°) or leaning against a wall' with the power switch on, in 'direct sunlight for 6 hours to a full day'; 'A proper full charge should power the unit for around 30 hours.'

findings.label: Backup charging
findings.value: Dual charging: a wall adapter keeps it running when sun is limited. Betta cannot charge at night but runs on stored power
findings.source_title: Can Betta run in cloudy weather, rain, or at night?
findings.note: Article modified 2025-12-09. It names the SE Plus as the model with dual charging, which implies the plain SE relies on solar alone. I could not open the SE product page or manual to confirm this (429 and 403 errors).

findings.label: How it charges when low
findings.value: Drives itself into sunlight for a 15-minute solar charge when the battery is low, then resumes cleaning
findings.note: Aiper's wording: 'When the battery runs low, the EcoSurfer S2 automatically moves to sunlight for a quick 15-minute solar charge.'

findings.label: Rated runtime basis and box contents
findings.value: 35 h, listed as 'Battery Life (Adapter Charging)'; 4-6 h charge time; DC charger included
findings.note: Aiper's 35 h rating is labelled as being from a full adapter charge, not from solar. The box list includes '1 × DC Charger'. The page showed no price.

findings.label: Sun needed to run nonstop (measured)
findings.value: About 5.7 h of full sun per day; overnight drain 3.46% of battery per hour
findings.source_title: Solar Pool Skimmers – Beatbot, Aiper, & Betta vs. Generic – The Hook Up
findings.note: The Hook Up worked this out from its measured overnight drain and solar gain. It saves power by stopping propulsion and keeping the front paddle running. This rival page is cited by ChatGPT, so it is context, not new.

findings.label: Sun needed to run nonstop and charger
findings.value: About 6.6 h of full sun per day; wall charger not in the box (+$25)
findings.source_title: Recommended Solar Pool Skimmers – The Hook Up
findings.note: The 6.6 h figure is from The Hook Up's test page. The recommendation page lists MSRP $429.00 and a common price of $339.00, which are not store prices from today.

findings.label: Solar panel and battery (reviewer)
findings.value: 24 W panel with SolarTrack, 10,000 mAh battery, rated up to 28 h without direct sun
findings.source_title: Beatbot Sora 70 and iSkim review – The Gadgeteer (Vincent Nguyen)
findings.note: Vincent Nguyen describes SolarTracking as 'light-chasing on the panel'. He does not say whether the robot parks in the sun when low. The 28 h figure is Beatbot's rating, not a measurement.
